ai: Artificial intelligence is a field about building systems that perform tasks such as finding patterns, making predictions, or generating text. This course explores how those systems learn, how to evaluate them, and where they can go wrong.
backend: Back-end development is the work behind an app’s screens: receiving requests, applying rules, and storing or retrieving data. For example, it can save a new goal and return your saved goals when you sign in.
c: C is a programming language that gives you direct control over memory and how a program works with the computer. It is used for operating-system components, device software, and other programs where low-level control matters.
csharp: C# is a programming language used with the .NET platform to build applications, web services, and tools. It is also used in game development with engines such as Unity; learning the language is separate from learning an engine.
cpp: C++ is a programming language used when performance and control over resources matter. Common uses include game engines, simulations, and systems software, but you can begin with small console programs.
css: CSS is a style-sheet language that controls how web pages look and fit different screens. Use it to set colors, spacing, fonts, and layouts—for example, arranging goal cards in a readable grid.
developer-toolkit: Developer toolkit is a practical topic track, not a programming language. It covers tools and habits for building software, such as using the terminal, tracking changes with Git, testing behavior, and finding bugs.
go: Go is a programming language often used for web services, network tools, and command-line programs. It includes tools for coordinating tasks that happen at the same time, such as handling several requests.
html: HTML is a markup language that gives web content its structure and meaning. Use it to describe headings, paragraphs, links, forms, and other parts of a page—not its visual styling or program logic.
java: Java is a programming language used for applications, server software, and large business systems. Java programs commonly run on the Java Virtual Machine, which lets the same compiled program work on different supported systems.
javascript: JavaScript is a programming language used to make web pages respond to people and changing data. It can also run outside a browser—for example, in server programs—with an appropriate runtime.
kotlin: Kotlin is a programming language used for Android apps, server software, and sharing code across platforms. It works closely with Java, so projects can use Kotlin alongside existing Java code.
php: PHP is a programming language especially suited to server-side web development. It can process a submitted form, work with a database, and generate the page sent to a browser.
python: Python is a general-purpose programming language used for automation, data analysis, web services, and AI work. You can start with a small program that organizes information or calculates a result.
r: R is a programming language and environment for statistics, data analysis, and graphics. Use it to explore a dataset, compare measurements, or draw a chart that helps explain a result.
react: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces from reusable pieces called components. For example, a goal card can show data and update when someone checks off a task.
ruby: Ruby is a general-purpose programming language used for scripts, automation, and web applications. Web frameworks such as Ruby on Rails use Ruby, but the language and the framework are separate things.
rust: Rust is a programming language designed for efficient software with strong checks on how memory is used. Common uses include command-line tools, network services, and systems software.
sql: SQL is a language for working with data in relational databases, where information is organized into tables. Use it to find, combine, add, or update records—for example, listing all unfinished goals in a category.
swift: Swift is a programming language widely used for apps on Apple platforms and also used for server software and command-line tools. For example, it can provide the logic behind a phone app’s screens and actions.
typescript: TypeScript builds on JavaScript by adding ways to describe the kinds of values your code expects. It helps catch mistakes before running a program and is converted into JavaScript for execution.
